Florentine statesman, diplomat, and political theorist of the Italian Renaissance. Born in [[Florence]], he served the Florentine Republic as secretary to the second chancery from 1498 to 1512, with responsibilities in diplomatic and military affairs. He rose in importance under the gonfaloniere Piero Soderini and represented Florence at the courts of powerful rulers. When the Medici retook power in 1512, he was expelled from his duties, soon afterward mistakenly suspected of treason, and sent into exile. A year later he took up the life of a political writer.

His most famous work is [[The Prince]], written around 1513 but not published until 1532, five years after his death. It advises rulers on acquiring and keeping power, drawing on observations of figures such as [[Cesare Borgia]], and argues that rulers must sometimes adopt unsavory policies when political necessity requires, in contradiction to classical political thought. His *Discourses on Livy* (composed c. 1517) favors republican government modeled on ancient Rome and has been said to have paved the way for modern republicanism.

The Prince has been controversial since its publication. Many commentators read it as a manual for would-be tyrants, and scholars such as Leo Strauss restated the traditional view of Machiavelli as a "teacher of evil"; others stress his empirical analysis of power, built on the concepts of *virtù* and *fortuna*. His name came to evoke unscrupulous acts. He is often called the father of modern [[Political philosophy|political philosophy]] and [[Political science|political science]], and influenced Enlightenment authors such as [[Jean-Jacques Rousseau]] and James Harrington.

Renaissance polymath and astronomer from Royal Prussia who formulated a model of the universe placing the [[Sun]] rather than Earth at its center. He was born in Thorn (Toruń), in Royal Prussia, a semi-autonomous, multilingual region of the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland, to German-speaking parents. His father was a merchant from [[Kraków]].

Copernicus studied mathematics and astronomy at the University of Kraków from 1491 to 1495, then canon law at the [[University of Bologna]], medicine at Padua, and took a doctorate in canon law at Ferrara. He was a mathematician, astronomer, physician, classics scholar, translator, governor, diplomat, and economist. From 1497 he was a canon of the Warmian cathedral chapter, managing church estates at Frombork. In 1517 he derived a quantity theory of money, and in 1519 he formulated an economic principle later called Gresham's law.

His heliocentric model held that Earth and the other planets revolve around a stationary Sun, with Earth also rotating daily on its axis. A similar model had been developed eighteen centuries earlier by Aristarchus of Samos, an [[Ancient Greek|ancient Greek]] astronomer, but Copernicus likely arrived at his independently. He set it out in [[De revolutionibus orbium coelestium]] (*On the Revolutions of the Celestial Spheres*), published in [[Nuremberg]] in 1543, just before his death and dedicated to Pope Paul III. The book triggered the Copernican Revolution and made a pioneering contribution to the [[Scientific Revolution]].

Federal republic in West Africa (pop., more than 242 million), capital [[Abuja]]. It lies between the [[Sahel]] to the north and the [[Gulf of Guinea]] to the south, covers 923,769 sq km, and borders [[Niger]], [[Chad]], [[Cameroon]], and [[Benin]]. It is the most populous country in Africa and the sixth most populous in the world. It has 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory; the largest city is [[Lagos]].

More than 250 ethnic groups speaking 500 distinct languages live in Nigeria. The three largest, the Hausa, Yoruba, and Igbo, together make up over 60% of the population. English is the official language. The constitution ensures freedom of religion, and the population is divided roughly in half between Muslims and Christians.

The region has hosted indigenous cultures, states, and kingdoms since the second millennium BC. The Nok culture, c. 1500 BC, is one of the earliest known civilizations in the area. Later states included the Hausa Kingdoms in the north and the Yoruba Empire of Oyo in the southwest. In the early 19th century the Fulani Jihads culminated in the Sokoto Caliphate. The modern state originated with British colonization, taking its present shape in 1914 when the Southern and Northern Nigeria Protectorates merged. The name comes from the Niger River.

Nigeria became independent on October 1, 1960. A civil war (1967–70) was followed by military rule, with an unstable democracy from 1979 to 1983, until stable democracy was established in 1999. The electoral commission has been criticized for lacking transparency. Nigeria is one of Africa's largest economies and belongs to the African Union, the Commonwealth of Nations, and OPEC.

Major north-flowing river of northeast Africa, emptying into the [[Mediterranean Sea]]. At 7,088 km it is the longest river in the world, although it carries much less water than the Amazon or the Congo. Its length was measured in 2009 by satellite imagery, from a source in Nyungwe National Park, Rwanda.

The Nile has two major tributaries. The [[White Nile]] is longer and is considered the headwaters; it begins near [[Lake Victoria]] and flows through [[Uganda]] and [[South Sudan]]. The [[Blue Nile]] begins near Lake Tana in [[Ethiopia]] and contributes over twice the water volume of the White Nile. They meet at [[Khartoum]], from which the river flows north through the Nubian Desert to Cairo and empties near Alexandria, forming a large river delta. The Nile has followed its present course for about 15,000 years. Its drainage basin spans eleven countries. Egypt and Sudan, largely desert, withdraw its water for irrigation.

The river was the foundation of Ancient Egyptian civilization. Annual floods deposited nutrient-rich silt that supported crops, and the Nile facilitated trade, communication, transportation, and governance. Upstream of the second cataract lay Nubia, home of the Kerma culture and the Kushite Empire. European explorations around Lake Victoria in the late 19th century located the source of the river.

Today the Nile is critical to the economies of Egypt and Sudan. Over a dozen dams have been built in the basin since the late 20th century for irrigation and electricity. They have altered the flood cycle and restricted downstream silt, causing the delta to shrink. Dams such as the Aswan High Dam and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam have been the subject of international disputes over water scarcity, safety, food security, and displacement.

Chemical element with symbol N and atomic number 7, a [[Nonmetal|nonmetal]] and the lightest member of group 15 of the periodic table, the pnictogens. At standard temperature and pressure two atoms bond to form N₂, a colorless, odorless diatomic [[Gas|gas]] that makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere, the most abundant chemical species in air. It is estimated to be seventh in abundance in the [[Milky Way]] and the [[Solar System]].

The Scottish physician Daniel Rutherford is credited with discovering nitrogen in 1772, calling it noxious air; Carl Wilhelm Scheele and [[Henry Cavendish]] did so independently. [[Antoine Lavoisier]] proposed the name *azote*, from the Greek for "no life," because it is an asphyxiant; the name remains in many languages and in compounds such as hydrazine. The English name derives from *nitrogène*, coined in 1790 by Jean-Antoine Chaptal.

The extremely strong triple bond in N₂, the second strongest in any diatomic molecule after carbon monoxide, dominates nitrogen chemistry. It makes converting N₂ into useful compounds difficult, yet decomposing nitrogen compounds releases large amounts of energy. Elemental nitrogen is usually produced from air by pressure swing adsorption. About two-thirds is used as an inert gas, for example in food packaging, and much of the rest as [[Liquid nitrogen|liquid nitrogen]] in cryogenics. Important compounds include [[Ammonia|ammonia]], nitric acid, organic nitrates, and cyanides. Synthetic ammonia and nitrates are key fertilizers, and fertilizer nitrates are key pollutants in the eutrophication of water systems.

Nitrogen occurs in all organisms, mainly in amino acids, nucleic acids, and Adenosine triphosphate. It is about 3% of the human body by mass, the fourth most abundant element after oxygen, carbon, and hydrogen.

Any document or media content that attempts, in good faith, to convey information only about the real world rather than being grounded in imagination. Non-fiction typically aims to present topics objectively on historical, scientific, and empirical information, although some ranges into more subjective territory, including sincerely held opinions on real-world topics. The term often refers specifically to prose writing, where it is one of two fundamental approaches to storytelling, in contrast to narrative [[Fiction|fiction]], which is largely populated by imaginary characters and events.

While specific claims in a non-fiction work may prove inaccurate, the sincere author aims to be truthful at the time of composition. Writers may use features such as graphs, diagrams, timelines, headings, footnotes, maps, and indices to help readers find information. Simplicity, clarity, and directness are among the most important considerations, and the narrative techniques of fiction are generally thought inappropriate.

The boundary with fiction is continually argued over, especially in [[Biography|biography]]; [[Virginia Woolf]] described the biographer's problem of welding the granite-like solidity of truth with the rainbow-like intangibility of personality. Knowingly including untrue information is usually regarded as dishonest. Some works, such as journals, letters, and magazine articles, can legitimately be either fiction or non-fiction. Publishers and booksellers sometimes use the term "creative nonfiction" for works with a more literary or intellectual bent.

By the author's purpose, the main genres are instructional, explanatory, discussion-based, report-based, opinion-based, and chronological recounting. Common forms include academic texts, history books, life writing such as autobiographies and diaries, criticism, news stories, documentary films, essays, reference works such as encyclopedias and [[Atlas|atlases]], textbooks, and [[User guide|user guides]].

Continent in the Northern and Western hemispheres, bordered by the [[Arctic Ocean]] to the north, the [[Atlantic Ocean]] to the east, [[South America]] and the [[Caribbean Sea]] to the southeast, and the [[Pacific Ocean]] to the south and west. It covers about 24,709,000 sq km, roughly 16.5% of Earth's land area and 4.8% of its total surface area. It is the third-largest continent by size after [[Asia]] and [[Africa]], and the fourth largest by population, estimated as of 2021 at over 592 million people in 23 independent states and territories, about 7.5% of the world's population.

Definitions vary. The continent includes the subregions of Northern America (Canada, [[Greenland]], the continental United States, Bermuda, and Saint Pierre and Miquelon) and Middle America (Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean). The UN statistics division recognizes three subregions: Northern America, Central America (which includes Mexico), and the Caribbean. In human geography the term often refers only to Northern America, and in regional trade agreements such as NAFTA it denotes Canada, Mexico, and the United States. The Americas were named after the Italian explorer Amerigo Vespucci by the cartographers Martin Waldseemüller and Matthias Ringmann; Waldseemüller's 1507 world map placed "America" on present-day South America, and mapmakers later extended the name northward.

It is unknown exactly how and when the first human populations arrived. People are known to have lived in the Americas at least 20,000 years ago, and various evidence points to earlier dates. The traditional theory holds that hunters crossed the Bering Land Bridge between eastern Siberia and present-day Alaska from 27,000 to 14,000 years ago; a growing viewpoint is that the first inhabitants sailed from Beringia some 13,000 years ago. The Paleo-Indian period followed the Last Glacial Period and lasted until about 10,000 years ago, when the Archaic period began. Norse exploration and colonization began in the late 10th century, with several settlements in Greenland and at least one in Newfoundland. From 1492 the voyages of Christopher Columbus brought a transatlantic exchange and migration of European settlers.

Colonization led to most North Americans speaking European languages such as English, Spanish, and French. The continent is divided linguistically and culturally into Anglo-America and Latin America, with large Francophone populations in Louisiana and Quebec. Significant indigenous populations retain pre-colonial traditions, and Latin America lies to the south. Canada and the United States are the largest countries by land area.

Extended work of narrative fiction, usually written in [[Prose|prose]] and published as a book. The word derives from the Italian *novella*, meaning "new," "news," or "short story (of something new)," from the Latin *novella*, a diminutive of *novus*. According to Margaret Doody, the novel has "a continuous and comprehensive history of about two thousand years," with origins in the ancient Greek and Roman novel, medieval chivalric romance, and the Italian Renaissance novella.

Writers have long distinguished the novel from the romance. M. H. Abrams and [[Walter Scott]] argued that a novel depicts society realistically, as in [[To Kill a Mockingbird]], while a romance emphasizes marvellous or uncommon incidents. Works of the latter kind, such as [[Mary Shelley|Mary Shelley's]] *Frankenstein* and [[J. R. R. Tolkien|Tolkien's]] *The Lord of the Rings*, are nevertheless commonly called novels. [[Herman Melville]] preferred the term romance, which should not be confused with the genre of romance novel.

Characteristics often cited include fictional narrative, literary prose, intimacy of experience, and length. Fictionality is commonly used to distinguish novels from [[Historiography|historiography]], though the criterion is problematic, since early modern historians also embellished. E. M. Forster suggested a novel should have at least fifty thousand words.

The earliest novels include Greek and Latin prose narratives from the first century BC to the second century AD such as Petronius's *Satyricon* and Apuleius's *[[The Golden Ass]]*. Harold Bloom credits Lady Murasaki's *The Tale of Genji* with anticipating Cervantes. Printed books in China led to vernacular classic novels during the Ming dynasty (1368–1644) and Qing dynasty (1616–1911). Miguel de Cervantes, author of *Don Quixote* (first part 1605), is frequently cited as the first significant European novelist of the modern era, while Ian Watt argued in 1957 that the modern novel was born in the early 18th century with Robinson Crusoe.

Use of nuclear reactions to produce electricity. It can be obtained from [[Nuclear fission|nuclear fission]], nuclear decay, and [[Nuclear fusion|nuclear fusion]], but the vast majority comes from fission of [[Uranium|uranium]] and [[Plutonium|plutonium]] in nuclear power plants. Decay powers niche applications such as space probes like [[Voyager 2]]. Reactors producing controlled fusion have operated since 1958 but have yet to generate net power.

Fission was discovered in 1938, and a self-sustaining chain reaction was confirmed experimentally in 1939. The first human-made reactor, Chicago Pile-1, achieved criticality on December 2, 1942, at the [[University of Chicago]] as part of the [[Manhattan Project]]. A reactor first generated electricity on December 20, 1951, at EBR-I near Arco, Idaho.  The pressurized water reactor, developed by the U.S. Navy for submarines, became the standard for power generation. The Obninsk plant in the USSR became the first to supply a power grid on June 27, 1954, and Calder Hall in England became the first commercial station in 1956.

Global installed capacity reached 100 GW in the late 1970s and 300 GW by 1990. The 1979 Three Mile Island accident and the 1986 [[Chernobyl disaster]] brought increased regulation and public opposition. Nuclear plants supplied 2,602 terawatt hours of electricity in 2023, about 9% of global generation and the second largest low-carbon source after hydroelectricity. As of November 2025, 416 civilian fission reactors operated worldwide with a capacity of 376 GW. The United States has the largest fleet.

Supporters point to one of the lowest fatality rates per unit of energy and to the absence of direct greenhouse gas emissions. The anti-nuclear movement cites radiological hazards and accidents such as Fukushima in 2011, and contends that nuclear power is too expensive compared with alternatives.

Mathematical object used to count, measure, order, and label. The most basic examples are the [[Natural number|natural numbers]]: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and so forth. Numbers are represented in language by number words and by symbols called numerals; "eleven" is a number word and "11" the corresponding numeral. Because only a limited list of symbols can be memorized, a [[Numeral system|numeral system]] represents any number in an organized way. The most common is the [[Hindu–Arabic numeral system]], a decimal system that displays any non-negative integer using ten digits. Numerals serve for counting, labelling (telephone numbers), ordering (serial numbers), and codes (as with [[ISBN|ISBNs]]).

Over the centuries the notion of number was extended to include zero, [[Negative number|negative numbers]], [[Rational number|rational numbers]] such as one half, [[Real number|real numbers]] such as the [[Square root|square root]] of 2 and pi (π), and complex numbers, which extend the reals with a square root of −1 (i). Calculations use the operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and exponentiation; their study is called arithmetic, a term that may also refer to number theory, the study of the properties of numbers.

Bones with cut marks, possibly tallies, include the Lebombo bone (about 43,000 years old) and the Ishango bone (about 22,000 to 30,000 years old), though their interpretation as arithmetic artifacts is disputed. The earliest unambiguous numbers in the archaeological record are the Mesopotamian base 60 system (c. 3400 BC), with place value emerging in the 3rd millennium BC. The earliest known base 10 system dates to 3100 BC in Egypt. A Babylonian tablet of 1900–1600 BC gives 3.125 as an estimate of the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, possibly the oldest approximation of π. The Egyptians invented the first ciphered numeral system and the Greeks followed. Roman numerals dominated Europe until the Hindu–Arabic system spread around the late 14th century. Its key was the symbol for zero, developed by ancient Indian mathematicians around 500 AD.

The first known recorded use of zero as an integer dates to AD 628, in the *Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta* of Brahmagupta, who treated 0 as a number and gave rules for its use with positive and negative numbers. By 130 AD Ptolemy used a symbol for zero within a sexagesimal system. The Maya developed zero as a cardinal number, and the concept reached Europe through Islamic sources around the year 1000. The abstract concept of negative numbers was recognized as early as 100–50 BC in China, in *The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art*.
